description: What programs do, languages, flow of control

screens.body: A computer is a very fast, very literal follower of instructions. It takes input (what you give it), processes it (follows your steps), and produces output (the result). It never guesses, never gets creative — it does exactly what it's told, billions of times per second.
screens.heading: Computers follow instructions
screens.keyPoint: Input, process, output — exactly as instructed.

screens.body: A program is a set of step-by-step instructions that solves a problem — like a recipe. A recipe for jollof says: chop, boil, season, serve, in that order. A program does the same thing: do this, then this, then this, until the job is done.

options: Step-by-step instructions that solve a problem
check.question: A program is…

screens.heading: A program is a recipe
screens.keyPoint: Programs are ordered steps that solve a problem.

screens.body: Humans think in ideas; computers run on electricity. A programming language bridges the gap — it lets you write instructions in a readable form that can be turned into something the computer executes. Java is the language you'll use in this course: strict, popular, and everywhere in the industry.

options: Lets humans write instructions computers can run
Is spoken out loud to the computer
Only works on one brand of computer
check.question: A programming language…

screens.heading: Languages bridge human and machine
screens.keyPoint: Languages turn human ideas into runnable instructions.

screens.body: Before any code, there's the plan — called an algorithm. An algorithm is the step-by-step solution in plain words, no programming language needed. 'To find the biggest number: look at the first, compare with the next, keep the bigger one, repeat.' Good programmers plan the algorithm first, then translate it into code.

options: The step-by-step plan behind a program
check.question: An algorithm is…

screens.heading: Algorithms: the plan before the code
screens.keyPoint: Plan the steps first, then write the code.

screens.body: A program's flow of control is the order its instructions run. By default, it's simple: top to bottom, one line at a time. Later you'll learn to bend that flow — skipping lines with decisions (if), repeating lines with loops, and jumping to reusable chunks (methods). But the default is always: start at the top.

options: Top to bottom, one line at a time
check.question: By default, code runs…

screens.heading: Flow of control
screens.keyPoint: Code runs top to bottom unless told otherwise.

screens.body: Your Java code isn't run directly — it's compiled first. Compiling translates your readable code into a form the computer can execute quickly. If something's spelled wrong, the compiler complains before anything runs. Think of it as a strict editor that checks your work first.

options: Translates your code so the computer can run it
check.question: Compiling…

screens.heading: From code to running
screens.keyPoint: Compile first: translate, check, then run.

screens.body: Every programmer writes bugs — it's part of the job, not a sign you're bad at this. Debugging is the skill of finding them: read the error message (it usually points at a line), look at that line, and ask what you meant vs what you wrote. You'll debug daily as a developer. Get comfortable with it early.

options: Read the error and fix it — that's normal
check.question: When your program has a bug…

screens.heading: Mistakes are normal: debugging
screens.keyPoint: Bugs are normal; error messages point the way.
